topic.title: Education: Origins and daily operation in Community Learning Centres
topic.focus: how the initiative began and how it works each day

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-25. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: How it started
sections.text: In 2016 a bus company in Arequipa, a city in Peru, moved to a new office. It left an old yellow building empty. Rosa Mamani, a retired teacher, asked the company for the keys. She wanted a place where adults could learn to read. The company agreed and lent her the building for five years. Eight women came to the first class in August 2016. Today people call the centre Casa Amarilla, because these words mean the yellow house.

sections.heading: The classes
sections.text: Casa Amarilla teaches three subjects. The first is reading and writing for adults. The second is basic English, because many jobs in the city are in tourism. The third is a computer class, which started in 2019. Each class lasts two hours. Classes run in the morning and again in the evening, so students can come before or after work. About 180 adults study at the centre every year. The youngest student is 18 years old and the oldest is 79.

sections.heading: A day at the centre
sections.text: The centre opens at eight in the morning and closes at nine at night. There is always somebody at the front desk. From one to three in the afternoon the building is quiet, because the rooms are used for meetings. Students do not pay for their classes, but they pay a little for lunch. The teachers write the plan for the day on a small blackboard by the door. If a student misses two classes, a teacher sends a message to ask if everything is all right.

sections.heading: The teachers
sections.text: Nine people teach at Casa Amarilla. Two of them receive a salary and the other seven are volunteers. Most of the volunteers are students from the university, and each one teaches for one evening a week. Mamani is 68 years old now. She does not teach any more, but she comes every Monday to plan the week with the two paid teachers. Three of the teachers learned to read at the centre themselves. Julia Torres began as a student in 2017 and now teaches the morning reading class.

sections.heading: Money and the future
sections.text: Casa Amarilla is not expensive to run, but money is still a problem. A hotel in the city gives most of the money, and the families of students give small gifts. The agreement with the bus company finished in 2021, and the company now asks for rent. So the centre must make a decision in 2026. It can stay in the yellow house and pay more rent, or it can move to a cheaper building outside the city. Mamani says that many students would stop coming if the centre moved, because the cheaper building is far from the bus stop.

passage.full_text:
Paragraph 1 — How it started
In 2016 a bus company in Arequipa, a city in Peru, moved to a new office. It left an old yellow building empty. Rosa Mamani, a retired teacher, asked the company for the keys. She wanted a place where adults could learn to read. The company agreed and lent her the building for five years. Eight women came to the first class in August 2016. Today people call the centre Casa Amarilla, because these words mean the yellow house.

Paragraph 2 — The classes
Casa Amarilla teaches three subjects. The first is reading and writing for adults. The second is basic English, because many jobs in the city are in tourism. The third is a computer class, which started in 2019. Each class lasts two hours. Classes run in the morning and again in the evening, so students can come before or after work. About 180 adults study at the centre every year. The youngest student is 18 years old and the oldest is 79.

Paragraph 3 — A day at the centre
The centre opens at eight in the morning and closes at nine at night. There is always somebody at the front desk. From one to three in the afternoon the building is quiet, because the rooms are used for meetings. Students do not pay for their classes, but they pay a little for lunch. The teachers write the plan for the day on a small blackboard by the door. If a student misses two classes, a teacher sends a message to ask if everything is all right.

Paragraph 4 — The teachers
Nine people teach at Casa Amarilla. Two of them receive a salary and the other seven are volunteers. Most of the volunteers are students from the university, and each one teaches for one evening a week. Mamani is 68 years old now. She does not teach any more, but she comes every Monday to plan the week with the two paid teachers. Three of the teachers learned to read at the centre themselves. Julia Torres began as a student in 2017 and now teaches the morning reading class.

Paragraph 5 — Money and the future
Casa Amarilla is not expensive to run, but money is still a problem. A hotel in the city gives most of the money, and the families of students give small gifts. The agreement with the bus company finished in 2021, and the company now asks for rent. So the centre must make a decision in 2026. It can stay in the yellow house and pay more rent, or it can move to a cheaper building outside the city. Mamani says that many students would stop coming if the centre moved, because the cheaper building is far from the bus stop.
